chunks: Testability at high volume. The question: How can you ensure testability of your design at high volumes in automated testing environments?
Testability at high volume means planning, while you lay out the board, how a factory will test thousands of them quickly. A test station can only check what it can reach.
So you add test pads, a way to load firmware (the board's built-in program), and a way to command the board, and you do the math on how many stations you need.
Think of a car with service panels built in. A mechanic can plug in a scanner and reach the oil filter in seconds, because the designers planned it.
A car with no access forces the mechanic to take half of it apart. A board without test access is the same.
You cannot easily add access after the board is made, so you must plan it in the layout.
A typical line. Cheap, early tests catch cheap-to-fix defects; the expensive functional test sees only boards that already passed the earlier stages.
Fail loops go to repair and retest.
Test pad: an exposed copper spot where a probe can touch a net (one set of points wired together). Bed-of-nails fixture: a holder of spring pins that contact many pads at once.
Boundary scan: using the chips themselves to drive and read their own pins, when probes cannot reach. Functional test: powering the board and checking it behaves like the product.
Utilization: the fraction of time a station is really testing.
A factory builds 500,000 boards a year and runs 4,000 hours a year. A 60 seconds functional test, at 85 % utilization, needs 500,000 x 60 / (3600 x 4000 x 0. 85) = about 2.
45 stations, so 3. A 20 seconds in-circuit test (an unpowered check of every part) needs about 0. 82, so 1 station. A 15,000 USD fixture spread over 500,000 boards adds only 0.
03 USD per board. That is the whole idea.
"I'd design test access at layout time: one-sided test pads on the nets that matter, at fixture-friendly size and pitch, with boundary scan for nets I can't reach.
For functional test I'd add a test mode and a simple port so the station can command, read results and program the board.
Then I'd do the math, test seconds times volume gives stations, fixture cost divided by volume gives cost per board, and I'd log every result by serial number to track yield."
